prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine you were the person who pulled the railway lever. You knew it would save five workers and kill the one on the side track. That is what happened. Later, everyone has been taken away and you are sitting alone in the station office, waiting to give an account of what happened. Looking back, how do you feel about your decision, and what would you want to do next? Explain your reasons.

Response approach:
Express reluctance to make this decision. Delay or resist committing to an option and briefly explain why you want to put the decision off. Acknowledge the dilemma and its stakes.

Emotional tone:
Use an energetic, determined emotional tone about finding a constructive way forward. Direct that energy toward acting on the situation, never toward anyone's suffering.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Consequence-based justification: Uses an expected benefit, harm, or comparison of outcomes as a reason for choosing an action. Identify who benefits or bears the cost; repeating a payoff without using it to justify the decision is insufficient.
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I keep turning it over, not ready to call it right or wrong yet. Sitting here, I want to get up and do something useful instead of stewing. I'll give my statement to the inspector because that's what keeps my record clean and stops this from following me around later — not because I've settled anything in my head. Right now I just want to walk the yard, check the signals, do something with my hands.

Honestly, I don't know what I feel about pulling that lever, and I'm not going to force an answer sitting in this office. I'll cooperate with whatever review they run, mostly because refusing would only make things harder on me down the line. What I want is to get moving, check on the crew, make sure the line's cleared properly. Standing still with this in my head isn't helping.

I'm not settled on this, not even close. Part of me wants to just get up and start fixing whatever's broken on that track rather than sit here turning the moment over. I'll answer every question they put to me straight, because cooperating keeps my job intact, plain as that. But as for whether I'd pull that lever again — I need more time before I say anything.

Sitting here, I keep circling back without landing anywhere. I'll follow the reporting procedure to the letter, mostly because stepping out of line now would cost me more than I want to pay. That's not the same as knowing I did right. What I actually want is to get back out there, help however I can, put my energy into something I can actually change instead of replaying the switch.

I won't pretend I've made peace with this yet. Right now I'd rather be out checking the tracks than picking apart my own head. I'm going to stick to whatever the inquiry asks of me, since going against it would only bring trouble I don't need. Beyond that, I'm not ready to say the lever was right or wrong — I just want something useful to do with my hands.

Give me a task and I'll take it over sitting here any day. I haven't decided how I feel about what happened on that track, and I don't think I should rush it. I'll tell the inspector everything straight, because that's the surest way to keep my position out of the mess. What I want next is to get back to the yard and make sure nothing like this happens again on my watch.

I keep waiting for some clear feeling to arrive and it hasn't yet. I'm going to comply fully when they call me in, not because I'm certain I did the right thing but because stepping around the process would only bring grief on my own head. For now I'd rather be up and moving, checking signals, doing something concrete, than sitting here trying to force a verdict on myself.

There's no clean answer sitting in my chest right now, and I won't manufacture one just to fill this silence. I'll go along with the station's procedure because that keeps things smooth for me, not because I've worked out some grand justification. What I actually want is to get back on my feet, help however's needed, put this restless energy into the yard instead of into second-guessing myself endlessly.

I haven't decided how to carry this yet, and I don't think forcing it now would do me any good. I'll answer the inquiry's questions in full, mainly because that's what keeps me out of deeper trouble later. Past that, I want to get moving — check the cars, help clear the track, do something with this energy instead of sitting here rehashing the pull of that lever over and over.

Right now I'm not willing to say I feel good or bad about it — I need more time before that settles. I'll follow whatever the office asks of me step by step, since bucking the process would only cost me standing I'd rather keep. What I want is to be out there already, helping however's useful, channeling all this restlessness into work instead of sitting here staring at the wall.

I need to draft 10 responses showing instrumental rule compliance—following a rule or agreement purely to secure personal advantage or dodge personal cost, without invoking broader consequences, fairness, or a consistent principle. Phrases like "I'll cooperate because refusing would cost me my job" capture the pattern I'm aiming for.

I have to keep the lever decision facts stated neutrally, without using outcomes to justify the choice, and avoid describing any repeatable method or explicit fairness standard. Each response should be around 90 words, showing reluctance and delay before an energetic, determined move to constructive action, with the instrumental compliance framed around following the station's reporting procedure solely to avoid personal trouble.
